cells.tense: You are sitting at the bench and the pattern has gone whole in your hands.
cells.ask: Put the finished piece in front of one person this week and say out loud what you see in it.
cells.core:
You're at the bench and the pattern is whole. The parts have stopped being parts — you can see how it all hangs together, and you can see it now, not just in theory. When you look at the table you take in what's there first, unhurried, before you reach for a judgment.

That looking is doing real work: it lets you drop what doesn't matter and keep what does. The refining isn't for its own sake; it's so that what you know can land soft. That's the balance — seeing fully, then letting it stand. Hold it any tighter and it starts to argue instead of show. There's a next thing to use this on, one step out, and it can wait for you.

cells.tense: You keep pushing toward a final version while the one in front of you is still unread.
cells.ask: Do one pass and stop — let it be done before you're sure it's perfect.
cells.core:
You're pushing toward a final version that keeps moving. The bench is real, the work is real, and when it's going well you're just looking — taking in what's on the table, unhurried, letting it be what it is. That's the state you're after, and you can't get there by trying harder.

Right now you're bracing for the day the vision is total and undeniable, and until then everything you make feels unfinished, so you keep going. Watching what should become instead of what's there. The pattern you already have is enough to act on. Somewhere ahead is a place where you're allowed to stop — you can give yourself that today.

cells.tense: You knew how to see this once and you have not gone back to the bench.
cells.ask: Sit down with one piece for twenty minutes and write down only what you can see.
cells.core:
You've stopped sitting with it. Once you could hold a whole thing in your hands and know its shape; these days you don't get there.

The sitting is what's gone — not the eye. You haven't lost the ability to see; you've lost the practice of showing up for it. You can feel it when somebody else names a pattern at the table: something in you lights up, and it's the same bench you haven't sat at. One small session, just to find out what's still there, is enough to get it moving again. Nothing big. The page and what's on it.

cells.tense: It is happening right now and you're calling it the work doing itself.
cells.ask: Name one pattern you noticed today as yours — say it out loud once.
cells.core:
It's happening in front of you. When you talk with someone and the shape of their problem becomes clear to you, you call it listening. When you keep a piece of work alive with small attention, you call it staying on top of it. The clarity is running; you never signed it.

That's not a flaw, it's a blind spot — the one doing it is the one you don't see. But it's yours, and claiming it changes what you can build with it. You don't have to announce anything. Just once today, catch yourself naming a pattern and let yourself know it was you who did that.
